## Do court rulings change anything?

-   courts command neither the sword nor the purse, yet their rulings are treated as changing the world

-   this week: how decisions get executed, how much of their effect survives the politics, and what they do to behaviour, the economy and public opinion

-   how would we know that a ruling caused anything?

# Two streams

## How do decisions turn into outcomes? {.smaller}

-   two **streams** through which judicial decisions get executed

-   the **conveyor belt**: the relevant bureaucracy (civil service, police, prisons, registries) implements the decision mechanically

    -   execution depends on the **quality of implementing institutions**: capacity, professionalism, corruption

    -   the same quality determines how much compliance there is

    -   most decisions and arguably most of the impact courts have, but rarely studied

-   the **contested** stream: some decisions become contested or politicized

    -   execution still runs through the implementing institutions

    -   but impact now also depends on **other political actors** (executive, legislature, parties, other courts) and on **public support**

    -   compliance becomes a choice between implementation, evasion, override and backlash

::: notes
What moves a decision from one stream to the other? Salience, distributive stakes, who loses, media attention. The shadow effect sits upstream of both: some decisions never need executing because policy was adapted in anticipation. Support deterring non-compliance is the public-support arrow in the lower stream.
:::

## Two streams of judicial impact

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
flowchart LR
  D[judicial decision] --> Q{contested or<br/>politicized?}
  Q -->|no| I1[implementing institutions<br/>civil service, police, agencies]
  I1 -->|institutional quality| O1[execution and compliance]
  Q -->|yes| I2[implementing institutions]
  Q -->|yes| P[political actors<br/>executive, legislature, parties]
  Q -->|yes| S[public support]
  S -.-> P
  I2 --> O2[compliance, evasion,<br/>override or backlash]
  P --> O2
  S --> O2
```

# Compliance

## Compliance: concept and measurement {.smaller}

-   **compliance**: the addressee does what the ruling requires; **implementation**: the ruling is put into practice by whoever has to; **impact**: anything changes as a result, intended or not

-   two types of effects of courts in judicialized political systems: **direct** effects of litigation and rulings, **indirect** effects of anticipation and threat [@pavone2022shadow]

-   measuring compliance is harder than it looks: rulings differ in what they demand, addressees comply partially or late, and "full compliance" is often a judgment call [@kapiszewski2013compliance]

-   and compliance is endogenous: courts adjust their rulings to the political environment, so high compliance does not mean they are unconstrained [@vanberg2005politics]

## (Non-)Compliance

-   due to courts' enforcement-dependency, non-compliance is an attractive strategy for other actors (especially other branches of power)

    -   but non-compliance can itself generate more litigation

-   it is often less costly for the government/legislator to evade compliance implicitly

    -   e.g. creating a parliamentary working group but never delivering [@vanberg2001legislativejudicial]

## How courts secure compliance {.smaller}

-   **vagueness**: judges may write vaguer opinions where they fear defiance, hiding it from public view [@staton2008value]

-   **publicity**: courts use public hearings and press releases to draw public attention to their rulings [@krehbiel2016politics; @staton2006constitutional]

-   **monitoring**: the Costa Rican Supreme Court built and publicized a compliance monitoring system, after which its orders were implemented faster [@gauri2015costa]

-   in the conveyor-belt stream compliance depends on the bureaucracy, not on these tools

## Compliance with international courts {.smaller}

-   **domestic politics** shapes compliance with international courts

    -   new democracies implement ECtHR judgments faster at first, but the advantage reverses over time [@grewal2015are]

    -   compliance depends on domestic institutions, especially constraints on the executive [@hillebrecht2014power]

    -   media attention to a ruling predicts whether it is complied with [@reis2025media]

    -   leaders comply less with Inter-American Court rulings implicating a popular military as elections near [@parente2025domestic]

## Judgments waiting to be implemented {.smaller}

-   at the end of 2025, 3,889 ECtHR cases were pending full implementation, 1,162 of them "leading" cases that require a change in law or practice [@councilofeurope2026supervision]

-   949 cases were closed in 2025 and 921 arrived, so the stock barely shrank while leading cases kept rising

-   another 3,025 cases against Russia, expelled in 2022, make up almost 44% of the total, with over three billion euros unpaid

-   Russia, Turkey and Ukraine have the most pending leading cases

-   Romania cut its stock the most in 2025, which the Committee links to better-resourced national coordination

-   implementation of international judgments runs through domestic parliaments, ministries and courts

# The hollow hope

## The hollow hope debate {.smaller}

-   **the constrained court**: courts lack the tools to produce social change; *Brown* did little for desegregation until Congress and the executive acted a decade later [@rosenberg2023hollow]

-   **the dynamic court**: litigation works indirectly, by legitimizing claims, mobilizing movements and raising rights consciousness [@mccann1992reform]

-   **the backlash thesis**: *Brown* mattered, but by radicalizing Southern politics and provoking the violence that made civil rights legislation possible [@klarman1994how]

-   three claims about the same ruling; the disagreement is partly about which outcome counts as impact and over what horizon

## Four kinds of impact {.smaller}

|  | material | symbolic |
|------|------|------|
| **direct** | the addressees do what the ruling orders: policy adopted, prisoners released, payments made | the litigants and beneficiaries come to frame the issue as a matter of rights |
| **indirect** | agencies and NGOs not addressed by the ruling join in and form coalitions | the wider public debate and the media reframe the problem |

-   typology from the study of Colombia's T-025 ruling on displaced people [@rodriguezgaravito2015radical; @rodriguezgaravito2011beyond]

-   most impact studies measure the top-left cell; the other three are where Rosenberg and McCann disagree

## Process tracing {.smaller}

-   some effects of courts leave no ruling behind

    -   e.g. policy changed in anticipation of review (the **shadow effect**)

-   **process tracing** follows one case step by step through documents, interviews and timing [@collier2011understanding]

    -   a Norwegian welfare reform preempted review by a little-known international court [@pavone2022shadow]

    -   political entrepreneurs captured Guatemala's courts through the nomination process [@moralesforte2025entrepreneurial]

-   does each step leave the predicted evidence? does a rival explanation fit too?

-   one case reveals a mechanism; @martinsen2015judicial pairs case studies with a dataset

## Structural rulings {.smaller}

-   some rulings order a whole policy rather than a remedy for one claimant

    -   Colombia's T-025 on displaced people (2004), Brazil's declaration of an "unconstitutional state of affairs" in its prisons (2015), South Africa's order to provide nevirapine against mother-to-child HIV transmission (2002), India's right-to-food orders (from 2001)

-   the court usually keeps the case open and supervises it through hearings, reporting duties and deadlines

    -   South Africa's court set no deadlines or follow-up proceedings in *TAC* [@rodriguezgaravito2011beyond]

-   implementation runs through ministries and budgets, so these rulings sit in the contested stream from the start

-   T-025 reshaped displacement policy, budgets and framing, but displaced people's living conditions improved little beyond health and education [@rodriguezgaravito2011beyond]

## The limits of judicialization {.smaller}

-   judicial empowerment is usually pursued with the hope of increasing government accountability and individual rights protection

-   @botero2022limits argue that in Latin America, judicialization often fell short of these promises due to

    -   weak state capacity limiting the desired positive impact of courts

    -   weak social embeddedness of (liberal) legal structures

    -   corruption, nepotism and other pathologies inside the judiciary

::: notes
judicialization in Latin America as a product of the 1980s and 1990s liberal (either domestic or foreign) visions, out of step with local structures of support

in Lava Jato Brazilian prosecutors and judges were coming up with creative legal solutions; this opens them up even further to criticism
:::

# What rulings do

## What rulings do {.smaller}

| ruling or decision | outcome | effect |
|---------------------|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| *Dobbs* (2022) | births | up about 2.3% in states that banned abortion [@dench2024effects] |
| *Dobbs* | support for the Supreme Court | fell and stayed lower into 2023 [@levendusky2024has; @gibson2025do] |
| *Shelby County* (2013) | Black turnout | fell relative to white turnout in formerly covered areas [@billings2024disparate] |
| *Citizens United* (2010) | elections | Republican gains in state house races [@klumpp2016business] |
| *Obergefell* (2015) | social norms | shifted, but personal attitudes did not [@tankard2017effect] |
| CJEU *Junqueras* (2019) | euroscepticism in Spain | rose [@turnbulldugarte2022can] |

## Outside spending before and after *Citizens United*

```{r citizensunited}
read_csv("data/outside_spending.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cycle, y = spending_bn, fill = type)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2010, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 2010.2, y = 4.2, label = "Citizens United\n(January 2010)", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2004, 2024, 2)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Billion USD (nominal)",
       title = "Outside spending in US federal elections, 2004-2024",
       subtitle = "Total spending by groups other than candidates and party committees, by two-year election cycle",
       caption = "Source: OpenSecrets, Total Outside Spending by Election Cycle, Excluding Party Committees (archived 18 July 2026, accessed 19 October 2026)")
```

::: notes
the chart shows nominal dollars, and presidential cycles draw more spending than midterms
:::

## *Citizens United* (2010) {.smaller}

-   in January 2010 the Supreme Court held that corporations and unions may spend unlimited sums on independent political advertising

    -   two months later the D.C. Circuit's *SpeechNow* ruling opened the way to super PACs

-   outside spending by non-party groups tripled between the 2008 and 2012 presidential cycles [@opensecrets2026total]

    -   part of the rise is money switching channels, as spending on issue ads fell sharply after 2008

-   the ruling invalidated bans on corporate spending in about half the states, which supplies a comparison

    -   independent spending in state elections grew more than twice as much in these states [@spencer2014citizens]

    -   Republican chances of winning state house races rose in these states relative to the rest [@klumpp2016business]

## Judges' decisions and defendants' lives {.smaller}

-   the most literal impact of a judicial decision is on the person in the dock

-   as-if random assignment of judges turns a judge's leniency into an instrument for what happens next

    -   Norway: incarceration reduced reoffending and raised employment among those not working before [@bhuller2020incarceration]

    -   US: pretrial detention raised the probability of conviction and lowered employment years later [@dobbie2018effects]

-   the same design gives different answers because the decisions and prison systems differ

## Courts and the economy {.smaller}

-   in the classic narrative, independent courts constrain the executive's discretion, including to engage in arbitrary coercive acts, which benefits economic development [@north1989constitutions]

    -   across a sample of 104 countries, de facto (but not de jure) judicial independence is associated with higher growth rates [@voigt2015economic]

    -   externally funded judicial reforms raised powerless groups' belief that the president will not ignore the courts [@chemin2021can]

-   court quality has firm-level effects: comprehensive judicial reforms raise the productivity of firms in contract-intensive sectors [@chemin2020judicial]; less congested courts amplified the effect of Brazil's bankruptcy reform on credit and investment [@ponticelli2016court]

-   these are effects of judicial institutions rather than of particular rulings

# Rulings and public opinion

## Four public reactions to a ruling {.smaller}

-   **acceptance and legitimation**: a trusted court moves opinion towards the policy it upheld [@sternberg2022legitimacyconferring], helped by one-sided media coverage that backs the Court majority [@linos2016supreme]

    -   an international court builds support for compliance no better than international organizations or elites [@cohen2024judicialization]

-   **backlash**: the ruling moves opinion against it, as in Catalonia [@casas2024judicial] and after *Brown* [@klarman1994how]

    -   US public mood recoils from Supreme Court decisions at first, then moves towards the Court's positions [@ura2014backlash]

    -   yet advances in gay rights provoked no opinion backlash [@bishin2016opinion]

## Four public reactions to a ruling {.smaller}

-   **nothing**: *Bush v. Gore* left the Court's legitimacy intact [@gibson2003supreme]

-   **spillover**: the ruling changes what people think of the court or the polity rather than of the policy, as after *Dobbs* [@levendusky2024has; @gibson2025do], *Junqueras* [@turnbulldugarte2022can] and unpopular court decisions in a UK experiment [@ovadek2026contagion]


## Support for SCOTUS after *Dobbs* {.smaller}

-   even controversial decisions such as *Bush v. Gore* did not significantly reduce diffuse support for SCOTUS [@gibson2003supreme]

-   ... that is until *Dobbs* [@gibson2024losing; @levendusky2024has]

-   the fall in legitimacy lingered at least six months, though support may be starting to recover [@gibson2025do]

-   the incongruity for positivity theory: legitimacy was supposed to be resilient to unpopular rulings

## Rulings and attitudes {.smaller}

-   anti-gay bias fell faster after states legalized same-sex marriage [@ofosu2019samesex]

-   after Iowa's court ruling, people whose profile predicted support became more likely to back same-sex marriage [@kreitzer2014does]

-   *Obergefell* moved what people believed others thought, not what they themselves thought: rulings can shift **norms** without shifting attitudes [@tankard2017effect]

-   the opinion backlash that many predicted after gay-rights advances did not materialize [@bishin2016opinion]

-   rulings seem to change attitudes through perceived norms more than through persuasion
